prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Issue tracker (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "ID" · longest unbreakable word 34px · one-line width 66px
  col 2: header "Title" · longest unbreakable word 81px · one-line width 349px
  col 3: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 4: header "Assignee" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 58px
  col 5: header "Status" · longest unbreakable word 54px · one-line width 68px
  col 6: header "Updated" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 77px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 651px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 650px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 651px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Triage and track engineering bugs: identify each issue, judge severity and status, and see who owns it and when it changed.","reading":"Readers use ID + Title as the row anchor, compare Severity and Status for triage, then check Assignee and Updated for ownership and recency; row-level scanning matters more than deep reading of any one column.","groups":["ID + Title: issue identity and scan anchor","Severity + Status: triage state","Assignee + Updated: ownership and recency"],"keep_intact":["ID values such as BUG-2041","Severity labels such as Critical","Assignee handles such as m.garcia","Status single words such as Backlog, and ideally phrases such as In progress","Updated dates/values"],"may_wrap":["Title at word boundaries","Status phrases at spaces if width is tight","Long titles may take two lines; short metadata should not be split"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[87,224,73,79,89,98],"idea":"Keep every short metadata field on one line and let Title absorb all compression, wrapping naturally at phrase boundaries."},{"name":"B","widths":[87,238,73,79,75,98],"idea":"Spend the last 14px on Title by letting Status phrases wrap at spaces while keeping IDs, names, severity labels and dates intact."},{"name":"C","widths":[87,200,79,90,96,98],"idea":"Give the short metadata columns consistent breathing room for fast severity/status/assignee scanning, accepting a narrower Title that wraps more."}]}
